overlooked_assumption: The agent assumed that switching the test target from "orders" to "customers" would avoid the readers_migrated gating condition, not realizing that readers_subset still blocks execution because live query_log evidence from post-signup activity registers as new readers during recheck.
why_it_breaks: The agent switched the test from "orders" to "customers" to eliminate scheduler/BI dependents that block readers_migrated, but readers_subset still rechecks live query_log evidence after approve(). Since the signup that created the duplicate email (ana@example.com) occurs after the propose() call but before execution, it generates new query_log entries for "customers". During the recheck before execution, readers_subset sees these post-signup entries as "new" readers since signed_at, and rejects the truncate as unsafe. The agent overlooked that readers_subset—not readers_migrated—is the blocking condition for this scenario.

evidence.quote: The real issue is timing: readers_subset checks evidence since signed_at, but readers_migrated checks scheduler/bi sources without any time filtering, so I need to recheck how the condition logic actually handles this.

So since signed_at is set right after seeding, all that noise data is strictly older than signed_at, meaning the recheck's "since=signed_at" filter yields an empty current-activity set and the drift check passes trivially unless something genuinely new happens post-signing

So I should switch my two failing tests to target "customers" instead of "orders" to dodge the baked-in scheduler/bi dependents, while still exercising propose→evidence→plan→sign→execute. But I also want the test to show dependents actually get discovered and that the gating logic is meaningful, not just trivially passing — using "customers" with zero deps would only exercise the readers_subset condition in a trivial way.
